procedural_history.originating_court: Trial Court (inferred from the conviction for Section 304A of the Indian Penal Code)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 26.04.2017 of the High Court of Punjab & Haryana at Chandigarh in CRR No. 4113 of 2016.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Punjab & Haryana at Chandigarh, in Criminal Revision Application No. 4113/2016, upheld the conviction of the respondent for the offence under Section 304A of the Indian Penal Code but reduced the sentence from two years to eight months, subject to a prior deposit of Rs. 25,000/- towards compensation to be paid to the family/legal heir of the deceased.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State of Punjab, feeling aggrieved and dissatisfied with the High Court's judgment and order reducing the sentence, preferred the present appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 844 of 2023) to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal.

decision.sentence_status: The impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court reducing the sentence is hereby quashed and set aside. The sentence imposed by the learned Trial Court confirmed by the First Appellate Court is hereby restored.
directions: The accused be taken into custody to undergo the remaining sentence.
The accused is granted four weeks’ time to surrender.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in reducing the sentence imposed by the Trial Court and confirmed by the First Appellate Court.

facts: The accused, driving a Scorpio car rashly and negligently, overtook an ambulance from the left side, causing a collision.
The impact was so severe that the ambulance turned turtle.
As a result, one person died and two others in the ambulance sustained injuries.
The Trial Court convicted the accused under Sections 279 and 304A of the IPC and sentenced him to two years of rigorous imprisonment (RI).
The First Appellate Court (Sessions Court) confirmed both the conviction and the sentence.
The High Court, while upholding the conviction, reduced the sentence to eight months, citing the accused's poverty and status as a driver as mitigating circumstances.
law: The principle of just punishment is the bedrock of sentencing in criminal offenses.
Courts must award a sentence that is proportionate to the gravity of the offense and the manner in which it was committed.
The sentencing court must consider not only the rights of the accused but also the rights of the victim and society at large.
Showing undue sympathy to an accused by imposing an inadequate sentence undermines public confidence in the justice system.
The Indian Penal Code (IPC) is punitive and deterrent in nature, and deterrence is sometimes an imperative necessity.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had shown "undue sympathy" to the accused.
The High Court failed to properly consider the gravity of the offense, particularly the fact that the accused's rash and negligent driving resulted in one death and two injuries.
The High Court did not appreciate the severity of the collision, evidenced by the ambulance turning turtle, which indicated the high speed and negligence of the accused.
The Court held that considering the accused's poverty as the primary reason for reducing the sentence was a form of "misplaced sympathy," especially when it overshadowed the loss of an innocent life.
By reducing the sentence, the High Court failed to apply the principles of proportionality and deterrence, which are essential for such offenses.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in reducing the sentence. It found the High Court's decision to be unsustainable because it was based on undue sympathy and failed to consider the gravity of the crime. Consequently, the Supreme Court quashed the High Court's order on sentencing and restored the original two-year sentence imposed by the Trial Court.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in reducing the sentence imposed by the Trial Court and confirmed by the First Appellate Court.
appellant_arguments: The High Court seriously erred in interfering with the sentence imposed by the Trial Court and confirmed by the First Appellate Court.
The High Court showed undue sympathy to the accused when reducing the sentence.
The High Court failed to properly appreciate the manner in which the offence was committed, specifically that the accused's rash and negligent driving caused one death and two injuries.
The appellant cited the cases of State of Madhya Pradesh Vs. Surendra Singh (2015) 1 SCC 222 and State of Punjab Vs. Saurabh Bakshi (2015) 5 SCC 182 in support of their arguments.
respondent_arguments: The High Court acted correctly by considering mitigating circumstances when it reduced the sentence to eight months, subject to a prior deposit of Rs. 25,000/- for compensation.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The measure of punishment in a given case must depend upon the atrocity of the crime, the conduct of the criminal, and the defenceless and unprotected state of the victim. In imposing an appropriate punishment, courts must consider the rights of the criminal, the rights of the victim, and the society at large, so that the punishment befits the crime and reflects public abhorrence.
obiter: The principle of sentencing recognises the corrective measures but there are occasions when the deterrence is an imperative necessity depending upon the facts of the case.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court was not justified in reducing the sentence because it showed undue sympathy and imposed an inadequate sentence that was not commensurate with the gravity of the offense. The court failed to follow the established principles of sentencing, which require the punishment to be just, proportionate, and reflective of public abhorrence for the crime. By prioritizing misplaced mercy over the need for deterrence and the rights of the victim and society, the High Court's decision undermined public confidence in the efficacy of the law.
legal_tests_applied: The punishment must be adequate, just, and proportionate, commensurate with the gravity and nature of the crime and the manner in which the offence is committed.
The court must consider the social interest and conscience of the society, keeping in view the rights of the victim and society at large, not only the rights of the criminal.
The measure of punishment must depend upon the atrocity of the crime, the conduct of the criminal, and the defenceless and unprotected state of the victim.
The principle of sentencing recognizes corrective measures, but there are occasions when deterrence is an imperative necessity depending upon the facts of the case.
Imposing an inadequate sentence based on undue sympathy is impermissible, as it harms the justice system.
A meagre sentence imposed solely on account of lapse of time, without considering the degree of the offence, is counterproductive and against the interest of society.
policy_considerations: Justice demands that courts should impose punishment befitting the crime so that the courts reflect public abhorrence of the crime.
Undue sympathy to impose inadequate sentence would do more harm to the justice system to undermine the public confidence in the efficacy of law.
Awarding a lesser sentence encourages any criminal and, as a result of the same, the society suffers.
The court has a solemn duty to strike a proper balance while awarding the sentence, as society could not long endure under serious threats from crime.
If the courts do not protect the injured, the injured would then resort to personal vengeance.
Sentencing must have a string of deterrence inbuilt in it to care for and strengthen society's interests.
The common man will lose faith in courts if they do not appreciate the language of deterrence in cases involving cruel acts.
